Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: What do tokens know about their characters and how do they know it?
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained language models with subword tokenization encode character-level information, and through what mechanisms is this information acquired during training?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models with subword tokenization robustly encode character-level information in their token embeddings, and this knowledge is acquired through multiple mechanisms including systematic relationships between characters and syntactic features, as well as variability in tokenization.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models with subword tokenization implicitly learn substantial character-level information, and this knowledge arises from a combination of systematic form-function correlations in language and the inherent variability of subword tokenization.
papers.key_findings:
Subword-tokenized PLMs perform well above chance on a probing task to detect the presence or absence of specific characters in a token, with larger models generally performing better.
Character-level information is encoded across multiple alphabetic scripts (Latin, Devanagari, Arabic, Cyrillic).
Performance on the character probing task is partially explained by systematic correlations between certain characters and syntactic features (e.g., 's' with plurals, 'y' with adverbs).
Variability in how a word is tokenized across different contexts (due to case, whitespace, or misspellings) provides another mechanism for models to learn character-level information.
Character classification performance is better for rare letters and for characters appearing earlier in tokens, and is not solely driven by high-frequency tokens.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on static, non-contextualized embeddings rather than contextualized representations from later layers.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to contextualized embeddings from later layers of the model.
Investigate the implications of these findings for improving tokenization schemes, especially in multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) that use subword tokenization schemes can succeed at a variety of language tasks that require characterlevel information, despite lacking explicit access to the character composition of tokens. Here, studying a range of models (e.g., GPT-J, BERT, RoBERTa, GloVe), we probe what word pieces encode about character-level information by training classifiers to predict the presence or absence of a particular alphabetical character in a token, based on its embedding (e.g., probing whether the model embedding for "cat" encodes that it contains the character "a"). We find that these models robustly encode character-level information and, in general, larger models perform better at the task. We show that these results generalize to characters from non-Latin alphabets (Arabic, Devanagari, and Cyrillic). Then, through a series of experiments and analyses, we investigate the mechanisms through which PLMs acquire English-language character information during training and argue that this knowledge is acquired through multiple phenomena, including a systematic relationship between particular characters and particular parts of speech, as well as natural variability in the tokenization of related strings.

papers.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether other languages achieve comparable probing accuracy to English, whether they exhibit similar layer-wise behavioral patterns to English, and what the similarities are between probing vectors across different languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends probing techniques to a multilingual context and reveals significant disparities in LLMs' performance and representational qualities between high-resource and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and suggest that these models may not be learning deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages, especially low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages achieve higher probing accuracy than low-resource languages.
High-resource languages exhibit similar layer-wise trends to English, with accuracy improving in deeper layers, while low-resource languages show stable or only slight improvement.
Probing vectors of high-resource languages are more similar to each other, while low-resource languages have lower similarities among themselves and with high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Using machine translation to generate prompts and questions may introduce noise.
Only five open-source LLMs and two datasets are experimented with, limiting generalizability.
Only linear classifier probing is used; more sophisticated probing methods could offer deeper insights.
future_direction: Develop more equitable and effective multilingual language models that can better capture universal linguistic concepts.
Extend the research to multimodal models that incorporate visual and textual information.
Explore more sophisticated probing methods beyond linear classifiers.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques for large language models (LLMs) have primarily focused on English, overlooking the vast majority of the world's languages. In this paper, we extend these probing methods to a multilingual context, investigating the behaviors of LLMs across diverse languages. We conduct experiments on several open-source LLM models, analyzing probing accuracy, trends across layers, and similarities between probing vectors for multiple languages. Our key findings reveal: (1) a consistent performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages, with high-resource languages achieving significantly higher probing accuracy; (2) divergent layer-wise accuracy trends, where high-resource languages show substantial improvement in deeper layers similar to English; and (3) higher representational similarities among high-resource languages, with low-resource languages demonstrating lower similarities both among themselves and with high-resource languages. These results highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and emphasize the need for improved modeling of low-resource languages.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Discriminating Form and Meaning in Multilingual Models with Minimal-Pair ABX Tasks
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning), and how do these representations evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free ABX-style discrimination framework for analyzing multilingual representations, and shows that in XLM-R, language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers over training, while meaning discrimination increases and stabilizes in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: ABX discrimination metrics provide a lightweight, interpretable tool for analyzing multilingual representations, revealing that language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers while meaning discrimination increases in deeper layers, with implications for understanding cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers.
Meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers.
There is a negative correlation between language and meaning discrimination across language pairs and checkpoints.
Language discrimination negatively correlates with performance on form-sensitive tasks like POS and NER in cross-lingual transfer.
Meaning discrimination does not consistently predict downstream task performance.
papers.limitation:
Encoder architecture and single-model scope: only tested on XLM-R (encoder-only), not decoder-only or encoder-decoder models.
Discrimination vs Separation: does not explicitly quantify separation in the representation space.
Task coverage: only POS, NER, NLI, may not capture deeper semantic capabilities.
Cross-linguistic generality vs. language-specific phenomena: not investigating specific languages or families in detail.
future_direction: Linking discrimination patterns to typological linguistic features.
Evaluating deeper semantic tasks.
Applying ABX metrics to decoder-only LLMs and more recent multilingual models.
papers.abstract: We introduce a set of training-free ABX-style discrimination tasks to evaluate how multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning). Inspired from speech processing, these zero-shot tasks measure whether minimal differences in representation can be reliably detected. This offers a flexible and interpretable alternative to probing. Applied to XLM-R (Conneau et al, 2020) across pretraining checkpoints and layers, we find that language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers, while meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers. We then explore probing tasks, showing some alignment between our metrics and linguistic learning performance. Our results position ABX tasks as a lightweight framework for analyzing the structure of multilingual representations.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Steering into New Embedding Spaces: Analyzing Cross-Lingual Alignment Induced by Model Interventions in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the finding experts intervention on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: Intervening on language expert neurons in mLLMs projects embeddings into a new space with enhanced cross-lingual alignment, leading to improved performance on cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: The finding-experts intervention enhances cross-lingual alignment in mLLMs, improving retrieval performance, and is recommended for aligning representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The finding experts intervention shifts the embedding space, reducing distances between languages and increasing cross-lingual alignment.
Post-intervention, cross-lingual retrieval accuracy improves by up to 2x in top-1 accuracy.
Within-language similarity is preserved in the new embedding space, as shown by paraphrase retrieval accuracy.
Intervention on random neurons does not yield similar improvements, indicating the importance of targeting expert neurons.
The intervention is most effective when the model has been trained on both the intervention-target and the languages to be aligned.
papers.limitation:
Lack of access to training data and procedures for the models, limiting deeper analysis.
PolyLM-13b behaves as an outlier in the analyses, possibly due to training differences.
Only one intervention method (finding experts) is studied, leaving other approaches for future work.
future_direction: Explore the effect of intervention on alignment in controlled settings with known training data.
Compare different model intervention methods to understand their impact on representation space.
papers.abstract: Aligned representations across languages is a desired property in multilingual large language models (mLLMs), as alignment can improve performance in cross-lingual tasks. Typically alignment requires fine-tuning a model, which is computationally expensive, and sizable language data, which often may not be available. A data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning is model interventions -- a method for manipulating model activations to steer generation into the desired direction. We analyze the effect of a popular intervention (finding experts) on the alignment of cross-lingual representations in mLLMs. We identify the neurons to manipulate for a given language and introspect the embedding space of mLLMs pre- and post-manipulation. We show that modifying the mLLM's activations changes its embedding space such that cross-lingual alignment is enhanced. Further, we show that the changes to the embedding space translate into improved downstream performance on retrieval tasks, with up to 2x improvements in top-1 accuracy on cross-lingual retrieval.

papers.title: The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: An Underlying Mechanism for Language Latent Space Transitions in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: How do multilingual LLMs transfer representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space, and what neurons are responsible for this transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and empirically validates the Transfer Neurons Hypothesis, identifying specific MLP neurons that facilitate transitions between language-specific and shared semantic latent spaces in multilingual LLMs, and shows their critical role in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that transfer neurons are a key mechanism for latent space transitions in multilingual LLMs, enabling language-agnostic reasoning and output generation in the input language.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations in multilingual LLMs form language-specific latent spaces in initial and final layers, converging to a shared semantic latent space in middle layers.
Transfer neurons in the MLP module are responsible for moving representations between language-specific and shared latent spaces.
Type-1 transfer neurons shift inputs to the shared space, while Type-2 neurons shift outputs back to language-specific spaces.
Type-2 neurons exhibit language specificity and are similar to previously identified language-specific neurons.
Deactivating transfer neurons impairs representation alignment and reduces performance on multilingual QA tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have suggested a processing framework for multilingual inputs in decoder-based LLMs: early layers convert inputs into English-centric and language-agnostic representations; middle layers perform reasoning within an English-centric latent space; and final layers generate outputs by transforming these representations back into language-specific latent spaces. However, the internal dynamics of such transformation and the underlying mechanism remain underexplored. Towards a deeper understanding of this framework, we propose and empirically validate The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: certain neurons in the MLP module are responsible for transferring representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space. Furthermore, we show that one function of language-specific neurons, as identified in recent studies, is to facilitate movement between latent spaces. Finally, we show that transfer neurons are critical for reasoning in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Are Knowledge and Reference in Multilingual Language Models Cross-Lingually Consistent?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models recall factual knowledge for coreferential statements in a similar manner across languages, how does the mechanism work, and which factors prevent model consistency in multilingual settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual consistency of factual knowledge in multilingual models, identifying bottlenecks related to language characteristics and showing that explicit cross-lingual supervision (code-switching, word alignment) improves consistency more than scaling or instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights limitations in cross-lingual consistency of multilingual models and emphasizes the value of explicit cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for enhancing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-lingual consistency is lower for languages dissimilar to English in script, family, or geography.
A consistency bottleneck exists in specific middle layers of the models.
Vocabulary expansion offers only slight consistency improvements and relies on deep semantic alignment rather than shared scripts.
Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives significantly improve consistency, while instruction tuning offers limited gains.
Activation patching on feed-forward neurons based on IG2 scores can partially calibrate consistency at test time, showing a causal relationship.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual consistency should be considered to assess cross-lingual transferability, maintain the factuality of the model knowledge across languages, and preserve the parity of language model performance. We are thus interested in analyzing, evaluating, and interpreting cross-lingual consistency for factual knowledge. To facilitate our study, we examine multiple pretrained models and tuned models with code-mixed coreferential statements that convey identical knowledge across languages. Interpretability approaches are leveraged to analyze the behavior of a model in cross-lingual contexts, showing different levels of consistency in multilingual models, subject to language families, linguistic factors, scripts, and a bottleneck in cross-lingual consistency on a particular layer. Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives show the most promising results, emphasizing the worthiness of cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for both multilingual performance and cross-lingual consistency enhancement. In addition, experimental results suggest promising result for calibrating consistency in the test time via activation patching.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how factual knowledge is acquired and represented in multilingual language models, examining performance differences across languages, shared vs. independent representations, and mechanisms of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies three patterns of fact representation in multilingual language models—language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred—and reveals limited effectiveness of cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge and underscores the need for better representation learning and probing datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance varies across languages with moderate correlation to training data volume.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations based on neuron activity patterns.
Cross-lingual knowledge transfer is limited and often localized to geographically proximate languages.
Easy-to-predict facts include shared entity tokens and naming cues, reducing apparent cross-lingual transfer.
Active neurons for facts in low-resource languages are more distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R), and findings may not generalize to decoder-based models like BLOOM.
future_direction: Enhance cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs). In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge. Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT). We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts. We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: language-independent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them. Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs.

papers.title: Linguistic Neuron Overlap Patterns to Facilitate Cross-lingual Transfer on Low-resource Languages
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual capabilities of LLMs on low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language in Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL), and whether sharing neurons can facilitate cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BridgeX-ICL, a method to improve zero-shot cross-lingual in-context learning for low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language based on neuron overlap patterns and an HSIC-based similarity metric.
papers.conclusion: Explores whether sharing neurons can improve LLMs' cross-lingual performance on low-resource languages and proposes BridgeX-ICL, a language-bridge approach validated on multiple cross-lingual tasks and language pairs.
papers.key_findings:
Strong neural overlaps align with human linguistic taxonomy within language families, but do not consistently hold across families.
Overlapping neurons embody shared semantic information, regardless of the language within or between families.
BridgeX-ICL improves performance on cross-lingual tasks (BLI and MRC) across 15 language pairs by an average of 6.02% and 5.25% over zero-shot baselines.
English is selected as the optimal bridge in 9 out of 15 language pairs in LLaMA (7 out of 15 in Mistral), indicating high-resource, Latin-script languages tend to be the default bridge, but non-Latin script languages like Chinese also show potential.
papers.limitation:
Limited coverage of language pairs and tasks due to lack of comprehensive benchmarks for low-resource languages.
The proposed linguistic distance measurement is probe-data-induced, offering qualitative but not quantitative insights.
Bridge selection reflects training biases of LLMs, inevitably reflecting their training data distribution.
papers.abstract:
The current Large Language Models (LLMs) face significant challenges in improving their
performance on low-resource languages and urgently need data-efficient methods without
costly fine-tuning. From the perspective of language-bridge, we propose a simple yet effective method, namely BridgeXICL,
to improve the zero-shot Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL) for low-resource languages. Unlike existing works focusing on
language-specific neurons, BridgeX-ICL explores whether sharing neurons can improve
cross-lingual performance in LLMs. We construct neuron probe data from the groundtruth
MUSE bilingual dictionaries, and define a subset of language overlap neurons accordingly to ensure full activation of these anchored
neurons. Subsequently, we propose
an HSIC-based metric to quantify LLMs’ internal linguistic spectrum based on overlapping neurons, guiding optimal bridge selection.
The experiments conducted on 4 crosslingual tasks and 15 language pairs from 7 diverse families, covering both high-low and moderate-low pairs, validate the effectiveness of BridgeX-ICL and offer empirical insights into the underlying multilingual mechanisms of LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/
xuyuemei/BridgeX-ICL.

papers.title: RomanLens: The Role Of Latent Romanization In Multilinguality In LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs achieve multilingual capabilities, and specifically, what is the role of Romanization in multilingual processing for non-Roman script languages?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use latent romanization as a bridge for processing non-Roman script languages, with romanized representations appearing in intermediate layers and target words emerging earlier when translated into romanized script.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implicitly use Romanization as a bridge for non-Roman scripts, with latent romanization occurring in intermediate layers and Romanization serving as a structural link between language-agnostic concepts and language-specific output.
papers.key_findings:
Latent Romanization occurs in intermediate layers during multilingual next-token generation, with romanized tokens appearing before native script.
Semantic concepts are encoded similarly regardless of whether the input is in native or Romanized script.
Romanized target representations emerge 1-2 layers earlier than native script representations in translation tasks.
Latent romanization is observed across multiple non-Roman script languages (except Chinese).
The repetition task shows a higher frequency of latent romanization compared to translation and cloze tasks.
papers.limitation:
The specific mechanisms by which LLMs adjust their interactions over different timesteps during token generation are not fully understood.
Interpretability of non-Roman scripts at latent layers is limited when models use tokenization schemes that split characters into multiple bytes.
The selective occurrence and varying intensity of latent romanization across languages are not explained.
future_direction: Develop training strategies that enhance performance across diverse linguistic communities.
Extend the work to models with alternative tokenization methods for a more complete understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual performance despite being predominantly trained on English-centric corpora. This raises a fundamental question: How do LLMs achieve such multilingual capabilities? Focusing on languages written in non-Roman scripts, we investigate the role of Romanization—the representation of non-Roman scripts using Roman characters—as a potential bridge in multilingual processing. Using mechanistic interpretability techniques, we analyze next-token generation and find that intermediate layers frequently represent target words in Romanized form before transitioning to native script, a phenomenon we term Latent Romanization. Further, through activation patching experiments, we demonstrate that LLMs encode semantic concepts similarly across native and Romanized scripts, suggesting a shared underlying representation. Additionally, for translation into non-Roman script languages, our findings reveal that when the target language is in Romanized form, its representations emerge earlier in the model’s layers compared to native script. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of multilingual representation in LLMs and highlight the implicit role of Romanization in facilitating language transfer.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual language models, and can it be causally manipulated to affect the language of generated tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to systematically increase the probability of words from a target language in masked language modeling, but not specifically towards translation-equivalent words.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R have both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing (AlterRep) can be fruitfully applied to manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language (e.g., Spanish) in a template of another language (e.g., English) increases the probability of words from the target language and decreases the probability of words from the template language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language does not significantly increase the probability of the target word but makes the model more likely to generate words from that language overall.
The manipulation leaves words from a third control language largely unaffected, indicating specificity.
The results hold for both monolingual and code-mixed training data, and for language pairs with different scripts and families.
The findings provide evidence that multilingual models contain both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.limitation:
Techniques like INLP extract only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed for other properties.
The method is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is non-trivial.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility for tasks like machine translation.
future_direction: Exploring the use of more complex, non-linear methods (like those proposed by Ravfogel et al., 2022) for manipulating model representations.
Applying the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Translating the results into practical applications.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs.We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R).We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y. Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task.We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language.But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models.Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component.And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Encoders Learn Cross-lingual Representation?
papers.research_question: How do multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations without explicit cross-lingual signals, and what factors influence this process?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation provides a comprehensive analysis of how multilingual encoders like mBERT learn cross-lingual representations, identifying key factors such as parameter sharing, anchor points, and language similarity, and proposes methods like contrastive alignment to improve cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations through shared parameters and anchor points, but performance is uneven across languages, and explicit alignment can help. Future work includes scaling to more languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns cross-lingual representations without any explicit cross-lingual signal, achieving strong zero-shot transfer across a variety of tasks.
Parameter sharing and anchor points (shared subwords across languages) are crucial for the emergence of cross-lingual representations in multilingual encoders.
Not all languages are equally represented in mBERT; low-resource languages suffer from poor performance due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
Explicit alignment methods, such as contrastive alignment using bitext, can improve cross-lingual representations, but their effectiveness varies across models and language pairs.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exhibits high variance due to underspecified optimization, and data projection with self-training can constrain and improve transfer performance.
papers.limitation: mBERT performs poorly on low-resource languages due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Continue scaling multilingual encoders to more languages and larger models
Extend to multimodal multilingual models
Improve cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
papers.abstract: NLP systems typically require support for more than one language. As different languages have different amounts of supervision, cross-lingual transfer benefits languages with little to no training data by transferring from other languages. From an engineering perspective, multilingual NLP benefits development and maintenance by serving multiple languages with a single system. Both cross-lingual transfer and multilingual NLP rely on cross-lingual representations serving as the foundation. As BERT revolutionized representation learning and NLP, it also revolutionized cross-lingual representations and cross-lingual transfer. Multilingual BERT was released as a replacement for single-language BERT, trained with Wikipedia data in 104 languages. Surprisingly, without any explicit cross-lingual signal, multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual representations in addition to representations for individual languages. This thesis first shows such surprising cross-lingual effectiveness compared against prior art on various tasks. Naturally, it raises a set of questions, most notably how do these multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations. In exploring these questions, this thesis will analyze the behavior of multilingual models in a variety of settings on high and low resource languages. We also look at how to inject different cross-lingual signals into multilingual encoders, and the optimization behavior of cross-lingual transfer with these models. Together, they provide a better understanding of multilingual encoders on cross-lingual transfer. Our findings will lead us to suggested improvements to multilingual encoders and cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Handle Multilingualism?
papers.research_question: How do large language models handle multilingualism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and verifies a three-stage multilingual workflow (MWork) in LLMs, introducing PLND to detect language-specific neurons and showing how fine-tuning these neurons enhances multilingual abilities.
papers.conclusion: The verified MWork explains how LLMs handle multilingual tasks and provides an effective method for language-specific enhancement through fine-tuning language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs convert multilingual inputs to English in intermediate layers for task-solving and then revert to the original language for generation.
Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection (PLND) can identify language-specific neurons without any labeled data.
Deactivating language-specific neurons causes significant performance drops in multilingual tasks but minimal impact on English.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons with small datasets (e.g., 400 documents) improves multilingual performance without compromising other languages.
The multilingual workflow involves understanding layers, task-solving layers for reasoning and knowledge extraction, and generation layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning with too many documents can lead to overfitting and performance deterioration due to disruption of original knowledge distribution.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse languages. This study explores how LLMs handle multilingualism. Based on observed language ratio shifts among layers and the relationships between network structures and certain capabilities, we hypothesize the LLM's multilingual workflow ($\texttt{MWork}$): LLMs initially understand the query, converting multilingual inputs into English for task-solving. In the intermediate layers, they employ English for thinking and incorporate multilingual knowledge with self-attention and feed-forward structures, respectively. In the final layers, LLMs generate responses aligned with the original language of the query. To verify $\texttt{MWork}$, we introduce Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection ($\texttt{PLND}$) to identify activated neurons for inputs in different languages without any labeled data. Using $\texttt{PLND}$, we validate $\texttt{MWork}$ through extensive experiments involving the deactivation of language-specific neurons across various layers and structures. Moreover, $\texttt{MWork}$ allows fine-tuning of language-specific neurons with a small dataset, enhancing multilingual abilities in a specific language without compromising others. This approach results in an average improvement of $3.6\%$ for high-resource languages and $2.3\%$ for low-resource languages across all tasks with just $400$ documents.

papers.title: Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics
papers.research_question: What causes cross-lingual factual errors in language models, and how can we understand and improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a controlled 'Petri dish' methodology to study cross-lingual knowledge transfer dynamics, identifies a crucial early phase where models develop unified or separate representations across languages, and shows that unification predicts cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggest new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Models undergo an early learning phase where they develop either unified or separate representations for the same facts across languages.
Unification of representations is essential for cross-lingual factual transfer.
The degree of unification depends on the mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract the language feature.
Cross-lingual transfer can be improved without increasing parallel data by manipulating data distribution and tokenization to reduce the language feature's representational footprint.
A unification score, measuring similarity of representations across languages, strongly predicts cross-lingual factual recall accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with cross-lingual knowledge transfer: they hallucinate when asked in one language about facts expressed in a different language during training. This work introduces a controlled setting to study the causes and dynamics of this phenomenon by training small Transformer models from scratch on synthetic multilingual datasets. We identify a learning phase wherein a model develops either separate or unified representations of the same facts across languages, and show that unification is essential for cross-lingual transfer. We also show that the degree of unification depends on mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract that language. Based on these insights, we develop methods to modulate the level of cross-lingual transfer by manipulating data distribution and tokenization, and we introduce metrics and visualizations to formally characterize their effects on unification. Our work shows how controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggests new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.

papers.title: Hyperpolyglot LLMs: Cross-Lingual Interpretability in Token Embeddings
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models (LLMs) represent relationships between languages in their input token embeddings? Specifically, does the geometry of these embeddings encode language identity or cross-lingual semantic similarity?
papers.core_contribution: The geometry of input token embeddings in multilingual LLMs is interpretable and differs between model families: XLM-RoBERTa embeddings encode language identity (writing systems), while mT5 embeddings encode cross-lingual semantic similarity without explicit parallel training.
papers.conclusion: Input token embeddings of LLMs are interpretable and meaningful, and mT5 accidentally achieves cross-lingual semantic alignment without explicit supervision, a goal that previously required dedicated methods.
papers.key_findings:
XLM-RoBERTa token embeddings linearly separate writing systems with 99.2% accuracy.
mT5 token embeddings have nearest neighbors that are often translations, with an average of 7.61 writing systems in the top 50 neighbors.
The geometry of token embeddings is consistent across parameter scales within the same model family.
mT5 discovers a shared cross-lingual semantic space without explicit parallel data or training objective.
The patterns in token embeddings are interpretable and differ by model family.
papers.limitation: The work is descriptive rather than explanatory; it observes patterns but cannot identify causal factors due to the many differences in model architectures, training methods, and pre-training corpora between LLM families.
future_direction: Explaining factors causing the different token embedding patterns (model architectures, pre-training procedures, data curation).
Exploring the utility of combining low-resource languages with closely related higher-resource languages in pre-training corpora.
Exploring potential applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in LLMs for downstream tasks and model selection.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer learning is an important property of multilingual large language models (LLMs). But how do LLMs represent relationships between languages? Every language model has an input layer that maps tokens to vectors. This ubiquitous layer of language models is often overlooked. We find that similarities between these input embeddings are highly interpretable and that the geometry of these embeddings differs between model families. In one case (XLM-RoBERTa), embeddings encode language: tokens in different writing systems can be linearly separated with an average of 99.2% accuracy. Another family (mT5) represents cross-lingual semantic similarity: the 50 nearest neighbors for any token represent an average of 7.61 writing systems, and are frequently translations. This result is surprising given that there is no explicit parallel cross-lingual training corpora and no explicit incentive for translations in pre-training objectives. Our research opens the door for investigations in 1) The effect of pre-training and model architectures on representations of languages and 2) The applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in language models.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: On the Multilingual Ability of Decoder-based Pre-trained Language Models: Finding and Controlling Language-Specific Neurons
papers.research_question: How do decoder-based pre-trained language models handle multilingualism? Specifically, do language-specific neurons exist and how can they be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the existence of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs and shows that intervening on these neurons can control the language of generated text.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the activity of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs, showing their existence and controllability, which can facilitate deeper understanding and future research.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons are unique to each language with little overlap (<5%).
These neurons are mainly distributed in the first and last few layers of the model.
Intervening on a small set of language-specific neurons (top and bottom 1000) can drastically change the probability of generating text in the target language.
The distribution pattern of language-specific neurons is consistent across languages and model variants.
For conditional text generation (machine translation), intervention on language-specific neurons can improve translation accuracy and BLEU score for some models (like Llama2).
papers.limitation:
Only analyzes open models with publicly available parameters, not closed models like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
Focuses on only six languages; other languages need to be examined in future studies.
Does not analyze encoder-decoder-based PLMs (e.g., mT5) due to architectural differences.
future_direction: Proposing language-specific model-compression methods.
Proposing new fine-tuning methods for downstream tasks to facilitate generalization to languages not included in the training dataset (e.g., only fine-tuning the middle-layer parameters).
Analysis of encoder-decoder-based PLMs remains important for future work.
papers.abstract: Current decoder-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) successfully demonstrate multilingual capabilities. However, it is unclear how these models handle multilingualism. We analyze the neuron-level internal behavior of multilingual decoder-based PLMs, Specifically examining the existence of neurons that fire ``uniquely for each language'' within decoder-only multilingual PLMs. We analyze six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese, and show that language-specific neurons are unique, with a slight overlap (< 5%) between languages. These neurons are mainly distributed in the models' first and last few layers. This trend remains consistent across languages and models. Additionally, we tamper with less than 1% of the total neurons in each model during inference and demonstrate that tampering with a few language-specific neurons drastically changes the probability of target language occurrence in text generation.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
