Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: Semantic Pivots Enable Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to quantify, understand, and improve the cross-lingual ability of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a word-level cross-lingual translation task and dataset (CLWTD) to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies co-occurrence and semantic pivot behaviors in LLMs, links them to dataset co-occurrence, and shows that constructing a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset improves cross-lingual ability.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a word-level task to quantify cross-lingual ability, identifies and distinguishes two behaviors, attributes them to co-occurrence frequency, finds semantic pivots from the dataset, and improves cross-lingual ability by reconstructing a pre-training dataset.
papers.key_findings:
The Cross-Lingual Word Translation Dataset (CLWTD) provides a continuous metric that accurately reflects LLMs' cross-lingual ability.
LLMs exhibit two distinct behaviors during word translation: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior.
These behaviors are attributed to the co-occurrence frequency of words in the pre-training dataset.
Semantic pivots can be identified from the pre-training data and show a probability trend in intermediate layers.
Constructing a pre-training dataset with a high proportion of semantic pivots effectively enhances cross-lingual ability.
papers.limitation: Due to limited availability of open-source large language models with public checkpoints and pre-training data, experiments are only validated on the OLMo-1B model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable ability in cross-lingual tasks. Understanding how LLMs acquire this ability is crucial for their interpretability. To quantify the cross-lingual ability of LLMs accurately, we propose a Word-Level Cross-Lingual Translation Task. To find how LLMs learn cross-lingual ability, we trace the outputs of LLMs' intermediate layers in the word translation task. We identify and distinguish two distinct behaviors in the forward pass of LLMs: co-occurrence behavior and semantic pivot behavior. We attribute LLMs' two distinct behaviors to the co-occurrence frequency of words and find the semantic pivot from the pre-training dataset. Finally, to apply our findings to improve the cross-lingual ability of LLMs, we reconstruct a semantic pivot-aware pre-training dataset using documents with a high proportion of semantic pivots. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing cross-lingual ability. Our research contributes insights into the interpretability of LLMs and offers a method for improving LLMs' cross-lingual ability.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Isolating Culture Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we localize a set of neurons that drives cultural propensities in multilingual LLMs, separate them from language-specific neurons, and modulate them through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that culture-specific neurons can be identified in multilingual LLMs, are largely separable from language-specific neurons, and can be selectively modulated through interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cultural knowledge concentrates in specialized neuron populations predominantly localized in upper layers of multilingual language models and that pure culture neurons play a substantial functional role.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-specific neurons are largely separable from language-specific neurons.
Cultural representations are localized in upper layers of the model.
Different cultures are encoded in distinct neural populations with minimal cross-cultural interference.
Pure culture-specific neurons (not overlapping with language) constitute about 56.7% of culture-related neurons and are functionally important.
Ablation of culture-specific neurons increases perplexity on culturally relevant data, confirming their critical role.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to a small set of open-source models.
Methodology relies on entropy-based metrics and dataset sampling choices.
MUREL covers only six cultures, potentially omitting important cultural phenomena.
Evaluation focuses on neuron ablation and perplexity; future work should include more comprehensive behavioral and downstream assessments.
future_direction: Broadening coverage to additional cultures, languages, and models.
Extending localization to attention heads.
Testing sufficiency via activation scaling and steering, and evaluating intervention effects on downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Language and culture are deeply intertwined, yet it has been unclear how and where multilingual large language models encode culture. Here, we build on an established methodology for identifying language-specific neurons to localize and isolate culture-specific neurons, carefully disentangling their overlap and interaction with language-specific neurons. To facilitate our experiments, we introduce MUREL, a curated dataset of 85.2 million tokens spanning six different cultures. Our localization and intervention experiments show that LLMs encode different cultures in distinct neuron populations, predominantly in upper layers, and that these culture neurons can be modulated largely independently of language-specific neurons or those specific to other cultures. These findings suggest that cultural knowledge and propensities in multilingual language models can be selectively isolated and edited, with implications for fairness, inclusivity, and alignment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/namazifard/Culture_Neurons.

papers.title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs encode words internally from sub-word tokens, and if so, how.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally detokenize sub-word tokens into whole-word representations in early to middle layers via an inner lexicon, enabling vocabulary expansion without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The work unravels the word detokenization process in LLMs, showing it occurs in early to middle layers and enables practical applications for optimizing tokenization and inference costs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can distinguish words from nonwords, with the distinction emerging in early to middle layers.
The last token of a word (even if split) can be decoded as the full word, indicating an inner lexicon.
FFN layers are crucial for retrieving full-word representations from the inner lexicon.
Attention patterns show early layers aggregate sub-word tokens, then later layers ignore them as the full word representation forms.
The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how. We present evidence that LLMs engage in an intrinsic detokenization process, where sub-word sequences are combined into coherent whole-word representations at their last token. Our experiments show that this process primarily takes place within the early and middle layers of the model. We further demonstrate its robustness to arbitrary splits (e.g., "cats" to "ca" and "ts"), typos, and importantly-to out-of-vocabulary words: when feeding the last token internal representations of such words to the model as input, it can "understand" them as the complete word despite never seeing such representations as input during training. Our findings suggest that LLMs maintain a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer's scope. These insights provide a practical, finetuning-free application for expanding the vocabulary of pre-trained models. By enabling the addition of new vocabulary words, we reduce input length and inference iterations, which reduces both space and model latency, with little to no loss in model accuracy.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Interference in Multilingual Knowledge Editing through Null-Space Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently update knowledge in multilingual large language models sequentially across languages without causing negative interference and while preserving multilingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LangEdit, a null-space constrained framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that projects parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: LangEdit is an effective framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that uses null-space projection to isolate language-specific updates, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization, as demonstrated across multiple models and languages.
papers.key_findings:
LangEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in multilingual sequential knowledge editing, improving editing accuracy and multilingual generalization across three model architectures and six languages.
LangEdit effectively mitigates negative interference by projecting language-specific updates onto the null space of previous updates, preserving performance in previously edited languages.
The method demonstrates cross-lingual knowledge transfer, where edits in one language can be accessed in another without explicit editing in that language.
Editing effectiveness varies by language, with languages having less pretraining data (e.g., Spanish) showing greater improvement than high-resource languages (e.g., English).
LangEdit maintains high specificity, ensuring that edits do not affect unrelated knowledge, and improves downstream task performance on multilingual benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on 6-8B parameter LLMs; extending to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) could reveal scaling effects.
The current evaluation focuses on constrained editing scenarios; future work should explore a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Multilingual experiments are limited to 6 languages; developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages would better test the boundaries of LangEdit and baselines.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) to reveal scaling effects.
Exploring a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages.
papers.abstract: Efficiently updating multilingual knowledge in large language models (LLMs), while preserving consistent factual representations across languages, remains a long-standing and unresolved challenge.While deploying separate editing systems for each language might seem viable, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the need to manage multiple models.A more efficient solution involves integrating knowledge updates across all languages into a unified model.However, performing sequential edits across languages often leads to destructive parameter interference, significantly degrading multilingual generalization and the accuracy of injected knowledge.To address this challenge, we propose LangEdit, a novel null-space constrained framework designed to precisely isolate language-specific knowledge updates.The core innovation of LangEdit lies in its ability to project parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces.This approach mathematically guarantees update independence while preserving multilingual generalization capabilities.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across three model architectures, six languages, and four downstream tasks, demonstrating that LangEdit effectively mitigates parameter interference and outperforms existing state-of-the-art editing methods.Our results highlight its potential for enabling efficient and accurate multilingual knowledge updates in LLMs.The code is available at https: //github.com/VRCMF/LangEdit.git.

papers.title: How do languages influence each other? Studying cross-lingual data sharing during LM fine-tuning
papers.research_question: To what extent, and under which conditions, do multilingual language models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the use of Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods, specifically TracIn, to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level in multilingual language models, finding that models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that languages largely influence one another cross-lingually under various conditions, with cross-lingual sharing increasing during fine-tuning and languages playing both reinforcing and complementary roles.
papers.key_findings:
MLMs rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
Training samples from other languages can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.
The model exhibits different cross-lingual behaviour in zero-shot testing compared to when the test language is seen during fine-tuning.
Even with data imbalances, the model largely benefits from cross-lingual sharing.
For parallel datasets, cross-lingual sharing is high, and for non-parallel datasets, it is still observed but to a lesser extent.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limited the study to 125 test samples.
The method is restricted to relatively easy classification tasks and not generation or sequence labeling tasks.
The analysis focuses on the fine-tuning stage and does not disentangle pre-training effects.
future_direction: Extending influence function methods to sequence tagging tasks for more fine-grained analysis.
Studying the emergence of cross-lingual abilities during pre-training.
Inspiring future work on studying sharing mechanisms within multi-task and multi-modal models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) are jointly trained on data from many different languages such that representation of individual languages can benefit from other languages' data. Impressive performance on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer shows that these models are capable of exploiting data from other languages. Yet, it remains unclear to what extent, and under which conditions, languages rely on each other's data. In this study, we use TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020), a training data attribution (TDA) method, to retrieve the most influential training samples seen during multilingual fine-tuning for a particular test language. This allows us to analyse cross-lingual sharing mechanisms of MLLMs from a new perspective. While previous work studied cross-lingual sharing at the level of model parameters, we present the first approach to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level. We find that MLLMs rely on data from multiple languages from the early stages of fine-tuning and that this reliance gradually increases as fine-tuning progresses. We further study how different fine-tuning languages influence model performance on a given test language and find that they can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons: The Key to Multilingual Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models process multilingual texts, and what are the language-specific mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language activation probability entropy (LAPE) to identify language-specific neurons in LLMs, revealing that a small subset of neurons in top and bottom layers are crucial for multilingual processing and can be manipulated to steer output language.
papers.conclusion: The study provides evidence that language-specific neurons are key to multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and the LAPE method offers a way to identify and manipulate these neurons for better understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating language-specific neurons significantly impairs the model's proficiency in that language, as shown by increased perplexity and reduced generation quality.
Language-specific neurons are predominantly located in the bottom and top layers of LLMs, with bottom layers mapping inputs to a shared semantic space and top layers handling vocabulary mapping.
It is possible to steer the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons, mitigating off-target language issues.
Low-resource languages are centered around high-resource languages in the representation space, indicating dominance relations.
Neurons in larger models tend to be more specialized for single languages rather than shared among multiple languages.
papers.limitation:
The LAPE method is relative to the presence of multiple languages and cannot establish an absolute threshold for single-language scenarios.
Criteria for distinguishing between high-resource and low-resource languages within the model need further investigation.
Managing a large number of languages and differences between various languages requires future research.
future_direction: Enhance knowledge transfer between major and minor languages.
Devise efficient strategies for continual pre-training to accommodate specific languages.
Investigate the differences between various languages in the model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multilingual capabilities without being pre-trained on specially curated multilingual parallel corpora. It remains a challenging problem to explain the underlying mechanisms by which LLMs process multilingual texts. In this paper, we delve into the composition of Transformer architectures in LLMs to pinpoint language-specific regions. Specially, we propose a novel detection method, language activation probability entropy (LAPE), to identify language-specific neurons within LLMs. Based on LAPE, we conduct comprehensive experiments on several representative LLMs, such as LLaMA-2, BLOOM, and Mistral. Our findings indicate that LLMs' proficiency in processing a particular language is predominantly due to a small subset of neurons, primarily situated in the models' top and bottom layers. Furthermore, we showcase the feasibility to "steer" the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons. Our research provides important evidence to the understanding and exploration of the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Representing the bilingual's two lexicons
papers.research_question: Does the separation of lexical representations in bilinguals arise from functional independence in a single neural network rather than from architecturally separate systems?
papers.core_contribution: A single neural network can acquire and represent two languages functionally independently, with separation driven by language-specific input and inter-language similarity, without requiring architecturally separate systems.
papers.conclusion: The single network model provides a functional account of bilingual lexical representation and acquisition, explaining empirical data without innate architectural assumptions and accounting for similarity and frequency effects.
papers.key_findings:
A single network can store two lexicons even with sequential training, avoiding catastrophic interference when sufficient language-specific information is provided.
Functional independence of lexical representations in a single network depends on inter-language similarity, with more similar words showing less independence.
Within-language frequency effects can be observed in a single network, simulating human data previously taken as evidence for separate lexicons.
The model accounts for bilingual priming data, including effects of word similarity and frequency.
Second language learning in a single network does not require architecturally separate systems and can generalize within languages.
papers.abstract: A review of empirical work suggests that the lexical representations of a bilingual's two languages are independent (Smith, 1991), but may also be sensitive to between language similarity patterns (e.g. Cristoffanini, Kirsner, and Mi lech, 1986). Some researchers hold that infant bilinguals do not initially differentiate between their two languages (e.g. Redlinger &amp; Park, 1980). Yet by the age of two they appear to have acquired separate linguistic systems for each language (Lanza, 1992). This paper explores the hypothesis that the separation of lexical representations in biUnguals is a functional rather than an architectural one. It suggests that the separation may be driven by differences in the structure of the input to a comm o n architectural system. Connectionist simulations are presented modelling the representation of two sets of lexical information. These simulations explore the conditions required to create functionally independent lexical representations in a single neural network. It is shown that a single network may acquire a second language after learning a first (avoiding the traditional problem of catastrophic interference in these networks). Further it is shown that in a single network, the functional independence of representations is dependent on inter-language similarity patterns. The latter finding is difficult to account for in a model that postulates architecturally separate lexical representations.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.research_question: Can explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages enhance cross-lingual generalization in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) are implicitly alignable across languages in transformer LMs, and proposes a meta-learning method to explicitly align these concepts, improving zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual generalization without updating the LM parameters.
papers.conclusion: Explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages via meta-learning improves cross-lingual generalization, achieving competitive performance and narrowing the gap between languages, particularly for low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
Structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) can be identified based on prototypes in a relatively low-dimensional space of LM representations.
These structural concepts are highly alignable across languages in both encoder-only (mBERT) and decoder-only (LLaMA) models, as measured by RSA and Procrustes analysis.
A meta-learning-based method to align conceptual spaces achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on syntactic analysis tasks, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
The method reduces the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages.
The approach provides insights into cross-lingual in-context learning and can be integrated with prompting to improve generalization.
papers.limitation: Variations in alignability between language pairs may stem from insufficient UD treebank data for approximating prototypes and degenerate representation spaces for certain languages due to inadequate pretraining data or tokenization deficiencies.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to other aspects of language to better accommodate linguistic diversity using self-supervised knowledge.
Exploring more expressive probing models to extract structural concepts, especially grammatical relations, from models like LLaMA.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual masked language models encode morphological information, and where in the context does the disambiguating information reside?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an extensive multilingual morphological probing dataset and demonstrates that multilingual BERT models effectively encode morphological information, with a tendency for left context to be more informative than right context.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT models encode morphological information effectively, and the asymmetry in context reliance (left over right) is a general property of language, with exceptions tied to typological facts.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa achieve strong accuracy on 247 morphological probing tasks across 42 languages, outperforming an LSTM baseline.
XLM-RoBERTa's larger vocabulary makes it better suited for multilingual probing than mBERT.
Preceding context (left context) tends to hold more information for morphological prediction than following context (right context), which is surprising given the non-directional nature of Transformers.
Perturbation effects on probing accuracy correlate with language typological groups.
German is an outlier in the analysis, with different Shapley value distributions compared to other languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 42 languages dominated by Indo-European languages.
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce an extensive dataset for multilingual probing of morphological information in language models (247 tasks across 42 languages from 10 families), each consisting of a sentence with a target word and a morphological tag as the desired label, derived from the Universal Dependencies treebanks. We find that pre-trained Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa) learn features that attain strong performance across these tasks. We then apply two methods to locate, for each probing task, where the disambiguating information resides in the input. The first is a new perturbation method that “masks” various parts of context; the second is the classical method of Shapley values. The most intriguing finding that emerges is a strong tendency for the preceding context to hold more information relevant to the prediction than the following context.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: MPN: Leveraging Multilingual Patch Neuron for Cross-lingual Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we perform cross-lingual model editing to update knowledge in multilingual models so that edits in one language generalize to other languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple method for cross-lingual model editing by training multilingual patch neurons, which can be easily adapted to existing fine-tuning based editing methods to improve their cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: MPN is an effective method for cross-lingual model editing that enhances cross-lingual generalization while maintaining locality and reliability, requiring minimal changes to existing editing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Existing fine-tuning based editing methods possess a certain degree of cross-lingual editing effect, derived from the inherent cross-lingual transfer ability of the multilingual model.
The proposed MPN method improves cross-lingual editing performance without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology.
MPN achieves an average improvement of about 9% in CLG on the XFEVER dataset and about 12% on the XNLI dataset compared to baselines.
MPN demonstrates strong cross-lingual generalization and good locality, outperforming monolingual editing baselines.
The method is versatile and can be extended to other fine-tuning based editing methods.
papers.limitation:
The cross-lingual editing method is only applied to classification tasks (XFEVER and XNLI) and not to more complex tasks like question-answering.
The XFEVER dataset is created using machine translation without manual verification, which may affect translation quality.
future_direction: Utilize the Bi-zsRE dataset to assess cross-lingual editing performance on question-answering tasks.
Consider using larger models like GPT-4 to potentially improve translation results for dataset creation.
papers.abstract: Large language models are known for encoding a vast amount of factual knowledge, but they often becomes outdated due to the ever-changing nature of external information. A promising solution to this challenge is the utilization of model editing methods to update the knowledge in an efficient manner. However, the majority of existing model editing techniques are limited to monolingual frameworks, thus failing to address the crucial issue of cross-lingual knowledge synchronization for multilingual models. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that trains multilingual patch neuron to store cross-lingual knowledge. It can be easily adapted to existing approaches to enhance their cross-lingual editing capabilities. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments using both the XNLI dataset and a self-constructed XFEVER dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves improved performance in cross-lingual editing tasks without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology, thereby showcasing its user-friendly characteristics. Codes will be released soon.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: LINSPECTOR: Multilingual Probing Tasks for Word Representations
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate word representation models in a multilingual setting to understand what linguistic features they capture and how this correlates with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LINSPECTOR, a set of multilingual probing tasks and an evaluation suite for word representations, and shows that probing task performance correlates with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the introduced probing tasks and the LINSPECTOR framework are effective for evaluating word representations in multiple languages and that they correlate with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.key_findings:
Probing tasks can be used to evaluate word embeddings in multiple languages and show significant positive correlation with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
All embedding models achieved their lowest score for CharacterBin, a task that requires predicting the number of characters.
D-ELMo achieves the highest scores in probing for all language-test pairs, generally followed by fastText and GloVe-BPE.
Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
